resolution.note:
Both refuters killed every blocking finding, so the row stamps PASS:verify-refuted and this REVISE stays as the record. pedagogy §16 line 49: harm: I verified the quoted facts and they hold. Line 49 reads as quoted. Prompt 3 has no plan clause. Lines 25, 57 and 65 are as cited. I still refute the finding, for four reasons.

(c) The fix costs more than the defect.
- Prompt build-your-challenge-memory-3 is shared. `curriculum/exercises/apt101-build-your-product-memory.md` also embeds `{{prompt:build-your-challenge-memory-3}}`.
- That exercise already carries the plan gate in body prose as a runtime-fork toggle: "Turn on plan mode first... nothing is written until you say go", with a Cowork fork saying "Ask Claude to write a plan first".
- Adding "write a plan and wait for my approval" inside the shared prompt would stack a prompt-level gate on top of plan mode's own approval UI. That means a double approval, or a plan written twice, in the exercise that already gates correctly.
- `check_prompts.md` §10 and §39 establish that plan-mode-as-feature versus plan-as-ask is a runtime mechanic, handled by body and runtime forks or a `permission-mode:` chip. It is not a clause baked into a shared prompt body. §39 says to omit the chip when the mode is not load-bearing. The judge proposed neither the chip nor a fork. It proposed a shared-prompt body edit, which is the wrong remedy even if the rule applies.
- Any prompt-body edit also triggers the approval gate.

(d) Other lines already carry the gate.
- Line 21 is the heading "Approve the plan before the files change".
- Line 23 says "Ask for a plan first".
- Line 49 sits directly above the fence at line 51.
- Line 53 says "Your runtime may phrase the approval choices differently". This shows the gate is a runtime approval UI, not prompt text.
- Line 57 gives the review step. Git blame shows these were deliberately set in 6b15e39c and ab22d247 ("approve the plan before the files change") from a control-writer pass.
- The speed-runner scenario assumes someone skips a one-line instruction placed immediately above the fence, under a heading that names the gate.

(a) and (b) The harm is mostly a restatement of rule 16's "forcing functions live in fence" location clause, not a demonstrated consequence.
- A student who pastes prompt 3 with no plan still gets cited topic pages. Rules 1–3 in the prompt enforce sources-first and citations.
- Prompt 4's audit then catches problems.
- The worst case is that "Read the plan" has nothing to read. The student can notice that and ask for one.
- The taste note from the 2026-08-29 compaction pass records Antti saying students already use plan mode and that M2 "just does it better". That makes a prompt-level reminder a redundant tool explainer.

The line-65 reference is generic advice, not a control.

Rule 16 does apply in the abstract, but the finding does not survive the harm lens.
